To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) adolescents in the Netherlands report that the content of sexuality classes varies widely across schools, with the majority of schools covering anatomy and STI prevention, but few schools covering LGBTQ issues, (2) the extensiveness of the topics covered in sexuality classes was longitudinally related to an increase of perceived willingness to intervene in LGBTQ name-callings, and (3) female youth who reported having more topics covered in sexuality class reported fewer instances of being called names because of their sexual orientation.

the content and extensiveness of Dutch sexuality education, as reported by adolescents, is related to a decreased occurrence of LGBTQ name-calling, as well as an increased willingness to intervene in LGBTQ name-calls, by both teachers and fellow students.

the content of sexuality educations is not comprehensive enough and that a comprehensive sexuality education predicts a decrease in the prevalence of name-calling and a perceived willingness to intervene.

the content of sexuality educations and its effects on LGBTQ name-calling, perceived willingness to intervene in school, and school climate.
the content of sexuality educations in Dutch schools and the impact on LGBTQ name-calling.
the content of sexuality curricula in the Netherlands.

comprehensive sexuality education is related to an increase of perceived willingness to intervene and a decrease in LGBTQ bullying.

schools should not only focus on sexual diversity but also cover a wide variety of other sexuality-related topics in their sexuality education programs.

sexuality education is a valuable tool to promote the well-being and social acceptance of LGBTQ youth in schools.
